opus-5.5.text:
I think of the largest models as a kind of exploration frontier. When we train at a scale like PaLM, we sometimes see capabilities emerge that we simply didn't observe at smaller sizes: multi-step reasoning with chain-of-thought prompting, explaining jokes, translating between languages it saw relatively little of, or writing code from a fairly loose description. At first, those abilities look like they only exist because of scale.

But once you've seen a capability in a large model, you understand much better what it actually requires. You can ask: is this ability really about parameter count, or is it about the data mixture, how long we trained, how the prompt is structured, or whether the model saw enough examples of step-by-step reasoning? Often it turns out a good part of it is the latter. Then you can bring that capability down to smaller models through better data, longer training on more tokens, instruction tuning, or distillation, where the large model generates the rationales or examples that the smaller model learns from.

So the large model plays two roles. Scientifically, it shows us what's possible and gives us an existence proof. Practically, it can act as a teacher. I find that very encouraging, because it means the cost of training at the frontier isn't only paying for that one model. It's also mapping out the territory, so that more efficient, deployable models can follow behind and get much of the same benefit at a fraction of the serving cost.

That said, not everything transfers cleanly. Some abilities, especially very broad world knowledge or the most complex reasoning, still seem to benefit a lot from scale. Part of the research agenda now is understanding which capabilities are fundamentally tied to size and which ones we discovered at scale but can engineer more efficiently afterward.

r001.rationale: The response says that observing a capability in a large model helps identify what enables it, then describes reproducing it in smaller models through better data, training, instruction tuning, or distillation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, and I'd frame it as: the big model is often the discovery instrument, and the small model is the deployment vehicle.

When we trained PaLM, part of what we were doing was just asking, if you push scale far enough, what shows up? And a lot of the things people now take for granted, chain-of-thought reasoning, multi-step arithmetic, the ability to explain a joke, those didn't appear smoothly. They looked flat at smaller sizes and then kind of turned on past a certain threshold. If you only ever trained at eight billion parameters, you might have concluded that chain-of-thought prompting just doesn't work, because at that size it genuinely didn't help much. You needed the large model to even know the capability existed.

But once you know it exists, the problem changes. It becomes an engineering problem rather than a discovery problem. You know what the target behavior looks like, you can generate data that exhibits it, you can distill from the big model, you can train longer on better data, and you can design evaluations that specifically measure it. And what we've seen again and again is that capabilities that were "emergent" at five hundred billion parameters end up in models that are ten or twenty times smaller a year or two later. Not because the scaling laws were wrong, but because we stopped relying on scale alone to get there.

So I'd push back a little on the idea that these are two separate research tracks. The large model tells you where the ceiling is and what's worth chasing. Then the work on data quality, on instruction tuning, on distillation, that's what brings the floor up to meet it. Each generation of frontier models is, in a sense, writing the curriculum for the next generation of small ones.

The part I find most interesting is which capabilities compress well and which don't. Things that are more about format and reasoning procedure seem to transfer down pretty readily. Things that depend on breadth of knowledge, obscure facts, long-tail languages, those are much harder to squeeze into a small model, because there's just a limit to how much you can store. So I think the honest answer is that the big models will keep being where new things get found first, and the small models will keep inheriting a growing fraction of that, but not all of it.

r001.rationale: The response says the large model reveals that a capability exists, then describes reproducing it in smaller models through generated data, distillation, better training data, and targeted evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think of larger language models as a way to explore what’s possible. As we scale, we can discover capabilities that we didn’t know how to achieve before. Then the question becomes: does that capability really require a model of that size, or can we find a more efficient way to learn it?

Those are different questions. The scale at which we first observe a capability isn’t necessarily the smallest scale at which it can exist. Once we have an example of the behavior, we can explore better training data, different training methods, or distillation to help a smaller model achieve it.

So larger models can help us discover the capabilities, and that discovery can guide the work of making them more accessible and efficient. It doesn’t mean every capability will transfer easily, but it gives us a concrete target.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models can reveal capabilities and that observing one provides a concrete example to guide training data, methods, or distillation so a smaller model can achieve it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of larger language models as a way to explore what’s possible. As we scale, we can discover capabilities that weren’t apparent in smaller models, and then ask: What does it actually take to get that behavior? Is scale essential, or can we achieve it with better training data, a different training objective, or knowledge distillation?

So the larger model can help us identify a capability and provide a signal for teaching it to a smaller model. That doesn’t mean every capability will transfer, or that we fully understand why it emerged. But it gives us a concrete target. We can then work toward making that capability available in models that are less expensive to train and serve.

r001.rationale: The response says a larger model can reveal a capability, then asks what it takes to produce that behavior and names possible methods such as better data, a different objective, or distillation for teaching it to a smaller model.
